data.decision: The 21264 splits its integer execution resources into two clusters, each with its own set of integer ALUs, with results needing an extra cycle to move between clusters.
data.outcome: This clustered design allowed the integer execution units to run at high frequency, at the cost of a one-cycle penalty for results needed by the opposite cluster.
data.rationale: The paper's reasoning is that a single, fully unified integer issue/execution structure with full bypassing across all ALUs does not scale well with clock frequency, so splitting into clusters reduces wire lengths and bypass complexity, trading off an extra inter-cluster latency for higher achievable clock speed.
data.title: Clustered integer execution units
data.weakest_point: I recall the clustering concept and extra-cycle penalty as a real 21264 feature discussed in Kessler's paper, but I'm not fully certain of exact wording or whether alternatives are explicitly named as rejected.

data.decision: The paper describes sizing the out-of-order instruction issue queues (integer and floating point) to specific depths chosen to balance instruction-level parallelism extraction against the clock-cycle-time impact of larger, more complex issue logic.
data.outcome: The 21264 achieved a relatively deep out-of-order window for its era while still reaching high clock rates.
data.rationale: The stated reasoning is that larger issue windows can find more parallelism but the associated wakeup/select logic grows in complexity and delay, so the queue depth was chosen as a balance that could still support the target clock frequency.
data.title: Out-of-order issue window size vs. clock frequency trade-off
data.weakest_point: I recall this trade-off theme as characteristic of the paper's discussion but I'm not confident of specific queue-depth numbers or precise framing as an explicit rejected alternative.

data.decision: The paper describes replicating certain instruction-related structures (such as line prediction or pre-decode information) to support fast, high-bandwidth instruction fetch without creating a bottleneck.
data.outcome: The fetch mechanism (including a line predictor, a departure from a traditional branch predictor accessed at fetch time) supported high fetch bandwidth aligned with the processor's aggressive clock targets.
data.rationale: The rationale given is that a single shared structure feeding fetch/decode/rename would become a critical-path bottleneck as clock frequency increased, so replication or duplication of key fetch-related structures allowed parallel access and kept the front end from limiting overall pipeline throughput.
data.title: Instruction cache replication for register-mapping/rename purposes
data.weakest_point: This entry blends recollection of 21264's line predictor (a well-known but possibly imprecise memory) with an assumed 'replication' framing that I am not confident is explicitly discussed this way in this specific paper; direction of the actual decision is uncertain to me.

data.decision: The paper describes designing the 21264's microarchitecture with explicit attention to physical wire delay and floorplan layout, rather than treating physical implementation as a downstream concern after microarchitectural specification.
data.outcome: This physically-aware design approach is presented as necessary to achieve the processor's aggressive frequency goals.
data.rationale: The reasoning given is that at the target clock frequency, wire delays between functional units become a significant fraction of the cycle time, so microarchitectural decisions (like clustering) needed to account for physical placement and communication distances from early in the design process.
data.title: Wire-delay-aware floorplanning as a first-order design constraint
data.weakest_point: I believe this theme (wire-delay-driven design) is discussed in the paper given it's a well-known aspect of Kessler's writeup, but I cannot confirm precise phrasing or exact section placement.
data.where_in_paper: Introduction / design overview discussing physical design challenges

data.classic_trap: Assuming the reported short/open is a real physical defect and spending hours in the layout editor before checking whether it's an artifact of stale extraction decks, fill scripts, or a merged/aggregated multi-run report

common_root_causes.cause: Missing or malformed via/contact at a macro or block boundary (abutment stitching error)
Metal or dummy fill script accidentally bridging two nets or a fill exclusion region not applied
GDS layer/purpose mapping mismatch between layout and extraction ruledeck
Same-name net merge artifact from a multi-instance or multi-corner parallel LVS run mixing partial results
Genuine open due to a routing DRC waiver that removed a required via without an alternate path

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Re-run extraction/LVS on the same GDS with fill (metal/dummy) layers stripped out
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: fill-induced short confirmed if the short disappears once fill polygons are excluded
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: fill is excluded as cause if the short persists identically with fill removed

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Isolate the failing net(s) and view them in a layout viewer highlighted against the schematic connectivity, zoomed at the reported coordinate
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: confirms a real physical short/open if two unconnected shapes visibly touch or a required via/contact is missing at that coordinate
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: rules out a real geometric defect if the shapes look correctly connected/separated, pointing instead to an extraction or naming issue

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Re-run LVS with a hierarchical vs flat extraction setting (or vice versa) on the suspect block
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: hierarchy/black-box mismatch confirmed if the error appears only in one mode (e.g., flat merges two same-named nets across instances)
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: excludes hierarchy artifact if the failure is identical in both flat and hierarchical runs

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Diff the current GDS layer/purpose mapping table against the last known-good signoff mapping
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: layer-map error confirmed if a layer number was reassigned (e.g., a via layer mapped to the wrong GDS number) causing phantom opens
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: excludes layer-map cause if mapping tables are byte-identical to the last clean run

first_checks.check: Read the LVS tool's summary report for net count mismatch and short/open net lists before opening layout
first_checks.why_first: cheapest — text report takes seconds and immediately buckets the failure as shorts vs opens vs missing nets

first_checks.check: Check whether the mismatch count changed between the last clean run and this run by diffing extraction/LVS logs or checksums
first_checks.why_first: rules out whether this is a new failure from a recent layout/netlist edit vs a pre-existing latent issue

first_checks.check: Cross-reference the reported net names against recent ECO or metal-fill/via-fill script changes
first_checks.why_first: fill and ECO scripts are the most common source of accidental shorts/opens, so ruling this in/out early is high yield

first_checks.check: Confirm the extraction deck/rule file version matches the signoff version for this block
first_checks.why_first: a stale or mismatched extraction ruledeck can fabricate phantom shorts/opens that aren't real, cheap to rule out

data.node_era_note: at 7nm-and-below, double/multi-patterning coloring and complex via arrays make fill- and coloring-induced phantom shorts noticeably more common than at 28nm, where opens are more often genuine routing/via omissions
data.symptom: LVS mismatch: missing, shorted, or open nets

data.classic_trap: Chasing the reported W/L discrepancy as a real sizing bug when it's actually a device-merging/multiplier convention mismatch between the schematic netlister and the layout extractor

common_root_causes.cause: Stale or unmerged parallel device fingers/multiplier not matching schematic's device statement (M value mismatch)
Automated decap, ESD, or well-tap/filler insertion adding devices not present in the source schematic
PCell/generator parameter default drift between schematic symbol version and layout PCell version
Manual layout edit (hand-tweaked transistor for DRC/timing fix) not back-annotated to schematic
Comparing netlist and layout extracted from mismatched design revisions/tags

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Re-extract just the flagged instance in isolation and inspect its measured W/L against the layout ruler/measurement tool directly
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: real layout sizing error confirmed if the physically measured geometry disagrees with the schematic value
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: extraction/rounding artifact excluded from layout if the physical geometry actually matches schematic intent

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Toggle device parallel-merging (multiplier/finger combination) on/off in the LVS options and re-run on the flagged devices
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: confirms a merge-rule mismatch if extra devices disappear or sizes reconcile once merging rules match schematic's multiplier convention
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: excludes merge-rule cause if extra/mis-sized devices persist regardless of merge setting

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Diff the PDK device model/generator version used to build the schematic symbol against the version used for the layout PCell
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: PCell/generator version skew confirmed if the two were built from different PDK releases with different default parameters
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: excludes version skew if both trace to the identical PDK release and generator hash

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Search the layout for extra devices at the exact reported coordinates and check if they belong to an ESD, decap, or tap-cell insertion pass
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: confirms extra devices are from an automated insertion flow (ESD/decap/well-tap) if their location and type match that flow's placement pattern
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: excludes automated insertion if extra devices are in random hand-drawn areas with no relation to those flows

first_checks.check: Read the LVS property/parameter mismatch report to see which parameter (W, L, M, fingers) differs and by how much
first_checks.why_first: cheapest — immediately tells you whether it's a sizing tolerance issue vs a structurally different device

first_checks.check: Check whether the flagged devices are concentrated in one macro, one library cell, or scattered randomly across the block
first_checks.why_first: localizes whether the cause is a single bad library cell/generator vs a global extraction setting

first_checks.check: Confirm the schematic netlist and layout were both regenerated from the same design revision/tag
first_checks.why_first: rules out the most common trivial cause — comparing a stale netlist against updated layout or vice versa

first_checks.check: Check device parameter comparison tolerance settings (W/L rounding, multiplier merging rules) in the LVS run deck
first_checks.why_first: many size 'mismatches' are false positives from overly tight tolerance or differing merge rules, cheap to verify

data.node_era_note: at 7nm-and-below, multi-fin/multi-fin-pitch FinFET device declarations make finger/fin-count merging mismatches far more common than at 28nm planar, where W/L rounding tolerance was the dominant nuisance
data.symptom: LVS mismatch: wrong device sizes or extra devices

data.alternatives_or_rejected: Designing for high single-thread performance via deep pipelines, aggressive out-of-order execution, and high clock frequency, as in traditional high-performance processors
data.decision: Optimize the processor for aggregate throughput on commercial server workloads rather than single-thread performance
data.outcome: Resulted in a design with many simple cores and threads rather than a few complex high-frequency cores
data.rationale: Target commercial server workloads (web, database) exhibit high thread-level parallelism and memory latency-bound behavior, so many simpler threads can better utilize resources than one fast thread
data.title: Throughput over single-thread performance
data.weakest_point: The exact framing/wording of the throughput-vs-single-thread argument is not something I can reproduce precisely, though the general thrust is well established

data.alternatives_or_rejected: Complex out-of-order superscalar cores were rejected because their area and power cost would limit the number of cores/threads that could fit on the chip
data.decision: Use simple, single-issue, shallow (short) pipeline cores instead of complex superscalar out-of-order cores
data.outcome: Enabled 8 cores each with multiple hardware threads to fit within the chip's power/area budget
data.rationale: Given a fixed power and area budget, more simple cores with multiple threads yield higher aggregate throughput on server workloads than fewer complex cores
data.title: Simple, short pipeline cores rather than complex cores
data.weakest_point: I recall this trade-off being central to the paper but cannot verify the exact comparative language used against out-of-order designs

data.decision: Each core supports four hardware threads with fine-grained (cycle-by-cycle) thread switching to hide memory and pipeline stall latency
data.outcome: Improved core utilization and overall throughput despite each individual thread being relatively slow
data.rationale: Single-threaded execution on a simple, shallow pipeline would leave the pipeline stalled frequently on cache misses; interleaving multiple threads keeps the pipeline busy
data.title: Fine-grained multithreading per core to hide memory latency
data.weakest_point: I am not fully certain whether the paper specifies exactly 'four threads per core' versus this being from general Niagara/T1 knowledge

data.alternatives_or_rejected: Per-core private L2 caches and per-core dedicated floating-point units were implicitly rejected as inefficient given the target workloads' low floating-point demands and the benefit of a shared, coherent L2 for the crossbar-connected cores
data.decision: Use a single shared on-chip L2 cache banked and shared across all 8 cores, and a single shared floating-point unit shared among cores
data.outcome: Reduced chip area/power devoted to floating-point hardware and provided a unified coherent cache accessible to all cores via a crossbar
data.rationale: Commercial server workloads are integer-heavy with low floating-point usage, so a single shared FPU was sufficient, and a shared banked L2 simplified coherence among the many cores
data.title: Shared L2 cache and single floating-point unit design
data.weakest_point: The details of L2 banking and crossbar interconnect, and whether the single-shared-FPU rationale is stated exactly this way, may be blending with general T1 knowledge
data.where_in_paper: Cache/memory system and chip organization section

data.alternatives_or_rejected: Pursuing maximum single-core clock frequency at the cost of higher power draw was rejected in favor of a lower-frequency, higher-thread-count approach
data.decision: Explicitly designed for low power consumption relative to throughput delivered (performance-per-watt), influencing core simplicity and clock frequency choices
data.outcome: Paper reports a chip with substantially lower power consumption than comparable-throughput conventional processors of the era
data.rationale: Datacenter power and cooling costs made performance-per-watt a critical metric, not just raw performance
data.title: Power efficiency as a first-order design constraint
data.weakest_point: I am not confident the power/performance-per-watt argument is elaborated in this specific short IEEE Micro paper versus being more general Niagara marketing/architecture knowledge

data.decision: The paper describes using an Execution Trace Cache that stores decoded micro-ops in the order of program execution, rather than a conventional L1 instruction cache storing raw x86 instruction bytes.
data.outcome: The trace cache became a defining front-end feature of the Pentium 4, delivering decoded micro-ops directly to the execution engine.
data.rationale: The paper argues that decoding x86 instructions is complex and by caching decoded micro-ops instead of raw instructions, the processor avoids redecoding the same instructions repeatedly, improving front-end bandwidth and efficiency, especially since micro-ops are stored in execution order rather than program (memory layout) order, helping with branches.
data.title: Trace cache instead of conventional L1 instruction cache
data.weakest_point: I recall the general concept well but cannot confirm precise phrasing or exact placement of comparative reasoning against conventional L1I in this specific paper vs. it being general NetBurst knowledge.

data.decision: The paper describes a very deep pipeline (20 stages, as commonly cited) chosen to enable very high clock frequencies.
data.outcome: The Pentium 4 achieved much higher clock frequencies than its predecessor (P6-based) processors as a direct result of this deep-pipeline design choice.
data.rationale: The paper's stated reasoning is that a deeper pipeline with fewer logic gates per stage allows each stage to complete faster, enabling higher clock speed, which the design team viewed as important to overall performance.
data.title: Deep pipeline for high clock frequency
data.weakest_point: The exact number of pipeline stages (20) and whether this specific number is stated in this particular paper (vs. other Intel P4 papers/marketing) is uncertain to me.

data.decision: The paper describes staffed integer ALUs that run at twice the core clock frequency, allowing simple integer operations to execute and forward results faster than a single-cycle-per-clock design would allow.
data.outcome: This became known as the 'Rapid Execution Engine,' allowing very fast execution of basic integer ALU operations.
data.rationale: The paper's reasoning is that running the ALUs at double pump speed allows back-to-back dependent simple integer instructions to be executed with very low effective latency, improving throughput for common integer operations.
data.title: Double-pumped (double-speed) ALUs for integer execution
data.weakest_point: I am fairly confident of the general 'double-pumped ALU' fact but less sure exactly how the paper frames the trade-off/rationale versus just describing the mechanism.

data.decision: The paper frames the overall NetBurst microarchitecture design goal as targeting substantially higher clock frequencies over multiple future process generations, even if this meant lower per-clock instruction throughput compared to previous designs.
data.outcome: The paper presents this as the guiding philosophy behind NetBurst's architecture choices, including the deep pipeline and trace cache.
data.rationale: The stated rationale is that the design was intended to scale to much higher frequencies across several silicon process generations, with the expectation that raw frequency scaling would deliver strong overall performance over the processor's multi-year lifetime.
data.title: Prioritizing frequency headroom over IPC (instructions per clock) in overall design philosophy
data.weakest_point: This framing (frequency over IPC) is well known as NetBurst philosophy generally, but I am not confident this specific paper states it in these terms as an explicit trade-off versus simply describing the architecture; risk of blending in hindsight/general knowledge.

data.decision: Use a grid-based, deterministically-driven global clock distribution network to minimize clock skew across the chip
data.outcome: Reported low skew across the die enabling the target cycle time
data.rationale: Large multi-core chip required tight control of skew between the two cores and across functional units for timing closure at target frequency
data.title: Global clock distribution approach
data.weakest_point: I am not fully certain of the exact clock grid topology (mesh vs tree-of-grids) described, and may be blending in general knowledge of POWER-series clocking

data.alternatives_or_rejected: Fully synthesized/automated logic design for these macros was considered less able to meet the aggressive cycle time targets
data.decision: Critical high-frequency macros (e.g., execution units, register files) were hand-crafted using custom circuit design rather than relying solely on synthesized logic
data.outcome: Custom macros allowed the chip to hit its frequency targets in critical paths
data.rationale: Achieving the target GHz-class frequency required circuit-level optimization beyond what synthesis tools of the era could deliver
data.title: Use of custom circuit design in critical macros
data.weakest_point: The specific balance between custom and synthesized logic, and which units were called out, may not match the paper's actual wording

data.alternatives_or_rejected: Conventional master-slave latch structures were viewed as adding too much overhead per pipeline stage for the target frequency
data.decision: Adopted a pulsed-latch (LSSD-compatible) based pipeline latch design to reduce clock-to-Q overhead and support high-frequency operation
data.outcome: Enabled shorter effective cycle times while retaining LSSD testability
data.rationale: Reducing latch overhead was essential given the short target cycle time and deep pipelining of the design
data.title: Latch/pipeline circuit style for timing closure
data.weakest_point: I am not confident this specific latch-style rationale and comparison is explicitly stated in this paper versus being inferred from general POWER4/IBM circuit knowledge

data.alternatives_or_rejected: A flat, full-chip timing approach was implicitly rejected as impractical given chip complexity
data.decision: A hierarchical, unit-based floorplanning and timing-closure methodology was used, with independent timing budgets assigned to each macro/unit before chip-level integration
data.outcome: Enabled the design team to close timing across the chip through iterative unit-level and chip-level convergence
data.rationale: Chip-level complexity and the need for many engineers to work in parallel required decomposing timing closure into unit-level budgets that could later be integrated
data.title: Hierarchical floorplanning and timing closure methodology
data.weakest_point: Details of the specific budgeting/closure flow (tool names, iteration counts) are not something I can recall verbatim and may be generic to IBM ASIC methodology rather than paper-specific

data.decision: Power-conscious circuit techniques (e.g., selective use of lower-power circuit families, gated clocks) and floorplan-level power density management were employed to keep the chip within thermal/power budgets
data.outcome: Paper reports the design met its power/thermal targets for the given technology
data.rationale: High transistor density and clock frequency created power density concerns that had to be managed at both circuit and physical design levels
data.title: Power/density management via circuit and physical design choices
data.weakest_point: This entry is fairly generic and I cannot confidently attribute specific rejected alternatives or exact rationale phrasing to this paper specifically

data.alternatives_or_rejected: A single unified integer register file with 8 read and 6 write ports — rejected because its physical width would stretch the datapath and exceed the cycle-time target.
data.decision: Split the four integer units into two clusters (U0, U1), each with its own copy of the 80-entry integer register file (4 read / 6 write ports per copy), kept coherent with a 1-cycle cross-cluster write delay.
data.outcome: 21264 achieves 500–600 MHz cycle time; simulated performance loss from the inter-cluster delay is ~1%, and from static subcluster pre-assignment is 1–2%.
data.rationale: Fewer read/write ports per register file reduce datapath width so the register file does not become the cycle-time limiter; the 1-cycle inter-cluster penalty costs only ~1% performance per simulation.
data.title: Clustered integer execution with duplicated integer register files
data.weakest_point: The exact 1% / 1–2% simulation figures and the explicit '8 read / 6 write rejected' wording are corroborated by a contemporary Microprocessor Report article drawn from the same design team; the paper may phrase it differently.

data.decision: Pursue performance leadership by combining a uniquely high clock (500–600 MHz at 0.35 µm, six metal layers) with advanced out-of-order and speculative execution, while remaining software-compatible with prior Alpha generations.
data.outcome: 30+ SPECint95 and 58+ SPECfp95; 50–200% faster than 21164 on many applications while keeping the same 4-instruction fetch width.
data.rationale: A unique combination of high clock speeds and advanced microarchitectural techniques, including many forms of out-of-order and speculative execution, provide exceptional core computational performance.
data.title: Performance leadership via high clock speed + out-of-order, not brainiac-style widening
data.weakest_point: Whether the paper frames this as an explicit decision against a 'brainiac' alternative, or simply reports it as the achieved combination.

data.alternatives_or_rejected: A fully general pick-4 arbitration across all four units — not solvable within the target cycle time, so rejected.
data.decision: Size the integer issue queue at 20 entries, arbitrating up to 4 issues per cycle via two pick-2 arbiters (upper and lower subclusters), where each queued instruction may await at most two of the four integer units.
data.outcome: Up to 4 integer instructions issued per cycle; simulation used to quantify the performance cost of the pick-2 limitation and asymmetric arbiter.
data.rationale: The fundamental circuit loop (grant in cycle N, request in cycle N+1) must close within one cycle; a general pick-4 solution would not meet cycle time, so the design limits each instruction to awaiting at most two units, accepting some throughput degradation versus an ideal scheme.
data.title: 20-entry integer issue queue bounded by pick-2 arbitration circuit
data.weakest_point: The 'pick-4 not solvable' phrasing is most explicitly stated in a later physical-technology retrospective citing the 21264 issue logic; the IEEE Micro paper may describe it less bluntly.

data.alternatives_or_rejected: 8 KB primary caches as in 21164 — rejected because their small size caused high miss rates and frequent 6-cycle L2 accesses, hurting performance despite being single-cycle accessible.
data.decision: Implement 64 KB 2-way set-associative I-cache and 64 KB D-cache (each 2-way), augmented with a line predictor and a way predictor so that branch-redirect fetch can occur with no fetch bubble.
data.outcome: 21264 sustains 4 instructions fetched per cycle; cache miss latency to off-chip L2 is 13 cycles, with up to 8 outstanding misses.
data.rationale: Line and way prediction combines the advantages of set-associative behaviour with the fast access time of a direct-mapped cache, eliminating fetch bubbles and supporting 4-instruction-per-cycle fetch at 500+ MHz.
data.title: 64 KB primary I- and D-caches with line/way prediction to hide set-associativity latency
data.weakest_point: The 21164 8 KB comparison and 'rejected' framing comes from a contemporary Microprocessor Report article; the IEEE Micro paper itself may not state the 8 KB alternative as explicitly rejected.

data.classic_trap: Assuming a reported 'open' or 'short' is a physical route defect and re-routing/patching the layout, when it is actually a missing net label or a partition-merge artifact — or the mirror: quieting the error by adding a label/tie-off instead of fixing the real missing via or bridge.

common_root_causes.cause: Real open: missing via/contact or a route that failed to connect (e.g., ECO re-route broke an existing net).
Real short: unintended bridge in routing or metal sliver/dummy-fill bridging two nets.
Missing or misplaced net label (text) causing LVS to split one net into unnamed pieces (reported as open/missing).
Stale/mismatched source netlist or un-back-annotated ECO (net exists in one, not the other).
Distributed-LVS partition/merge artifact (phantom short or open at a partition boundary) or bad via recognition in the runset.

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Re-run LVS with a different partitioning seed and with one specific parallel extraction partition excluded from the merge (or run flat/non-partitioned).
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: short/open vanishes when that partition is dropped or with a different seed: merge/partition artifact, not a real defect
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: discrepancy persists in every seed/partition and in a flat run: merge artifact excluded; the net is genuinely shorted or open in the layout

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Trace the suspect net's extracted connectivity while ignoring net names/labels: check whether the metal is physically continuous versus whether the two pieces simply carry different or missing text labels.
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: metal is continuous but the pieces have different/missing labels: the 'open' is a net-naming/label-omission artifact, not a real disconnection
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: metal is physically disjoint (no connecting via/overlap): labeling artifact excluded; it is a real open (missing via or broken route)

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Re-run extraction/LVS with dummy metal fill, DECAP, and filler cells excluded or black-boxed from the comparison.
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: short disappears when fill/filler is ignored: the bridge is caused by dummy/fill geometry or an extraction rule merging fill into the net (phantom short)
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: short persists with fill/filler excluded: fill-induced phantom short excluded; it is a real route bridge or device/contact short in intentional wiring

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Cross-probe the missing net in the source: identify its driver and loads and whether the layout has the corresponding devices/placement.
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: net has no real driver/load in layout (tie-off, unconnected input, or instance never placed/ECO'd): source/intent mismatch or ECO omission, not an extraction defect
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: the net drives real loads present in layout but is absent from extraction: intent mismatch excluded; it is a missing route/label or extraction problem in the layout

first_checks.check: Confirm the LVS run compared the intended source-netlist revision against the current routed database (no stale netlist, no stale runset).
first_checks.why_first: cheapest; a stale source explains wholesale missing/extra nets and saves hours

first_checks.check: Read the LVS mismatch header: is it 'net missing in layout/source', 'short', or 'open (net split)', and are PG/well/global nets implicated?
first_checks.why_first: rules out the most severe class; PG/global shorts and opens are systematic, not random local defects

first_checks.check: Check whether every instance of a repeated cell/library cell shows the same net problem, or only one instance.
first_checks.why_first: a repeated hit points to the cell view, fill, or DECAP, not random routing

first_checks.check: Check if the suspect net has a real driver and load in the source, or is a floating/tie-off/unused net.
first_checks.why_first: cheapest way to see if a 'missing net' is harmless/unused rather than a defect

data.node_era_note: At 7nm-and-below, multi-patterning coloring errors, cut-mask/via-pillar extraction, and fill/dummy-induced or partition-merge phantom nets dominate, whereas at 28nm most opens/shorts are straightforward missing-via or route-bridge defects.
data.symptom: (7) LVS mismatch: missing, shorted, or open nets

data.classic_trap: The classic trap is editing the netlist (or waiving) to make an 'extra device' go away when the extras are physical-only cells the runset forgot to black-box; and for 'wrong size', changing the drawn W/L to match the netlist when the delta is just drawn-vs-effective rounding or finger counting — or conversely, waiving a gross 2x ratio as 'rounding'.

common_root_causes.cause: Physical-only cells (filler, decap, tap, endcap, antenna diode) in layout but not in netlist / not black-boxed in runset, reported as extra devices.
Stale source netlist or P&R optimization (gate sizing, buffer insertion, Vt swap) not back-annotated, giving wrong W/L/M or extra/missing devices.
Fingering / multiplicity convention mismatch: netlist says one device with N fingers or M=N, layout extracted as N parallel (or one wide) device.
Drawn-vs-effective parameter rounding or unit/measurement convention (sub-nm width rounding, gate-length bias, diffusion-shared W) giving tiny 'wrong size' deltas.
Leftover, duplicate, or DFT/scan-inserted instance in layout (ECO not removed, or partition-merge duplicate) creating a real extra device.

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Re-run LVS with physical-only cells (filler, decap, tap, endcap, antenna diode) explicitly black-boxed/ignored.
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: extra-device count drops to zero and remaining devices match: the extras were unmarked physical-only cells (runset/ignore-setup issue), not real logic
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: extras persist as named logic instances: physical-only-cell artifact excluded; there is a genuine extra instance in layout (or a device missing from the source)

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Toggle LVS parallel-transistor/finger merging (or compare extracted multiplicity) and re-run.
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: size/count mismatch disappears when fingers are merged (or not merged): it is a fingering/multiplicity counting convention between netlist and layout, not a drawn-size error
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: mismatch is invariant to the merge setting: fingering convention excluded; the W/L/M or device count really differs

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Measure the drawn geometry (poly width / number of fins) of the suspect device in the layout and compare it to the netlist parameter (times any bias/quantization).
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: drawn geometry matches the netlist parameter within rounding/quantization, yet LVS reports a different value: it is a drawn-vs-effective measurement or rounding/unit convention, not a real sizing error
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: drawn geometry is grossly different from the netlist parameter: rounding/measurement artifact excluded; the device is really drawn at the wrong size (Pcell parameter or manual edit)

discriminating_experiments.experiment: For an extra device with no source counterpart, inspect its connectivity: are all terminals tied to the same net/floating, or is it a scan/DFT/leftover ECO instance?
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: terminals are shorted/floating or it is a DFT/scan physical leftover: it is an unused/leftover instance that can be black-boxed, or the netlist is missing a physical-only view
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: the device is properly connected and drives logic: leftover/physical-only excluded; the source netlist is genuinely missing a device (incomplete netlist or failed ECO back-annotation)

first_checks.check: Read the device-mismatch summary: is it 'extra device in layout', 'missing device in layout', or a property mismatch (W/L/M/fingers) on a matched device?
first_checks.why_first: cheapest; separates count mismatch from size/parameter mismatch, which have disjoint cause sets

first_checks.check: Check whether the implicated devices are physical-only cells (tap, endcap, filler, DECAP, antenna diode) and whether the runset black-boxes/ignores them.
first_checks.why_first: rules out the most common systematic cause of extra devices; prevents debugging filler as logic

first_checks.check: Compare the magnitude of the size delta: tiny sub-1%/rounding difference versus an integer or ratio mismatch (2x W, different finger count, M-factor).
first_checks.why_first: rounding deltas are measurement convention; ratio mismatches are real parameter/Pcell errors

first_checks.check: Confirm the source netlist is the post-route/back-annotated version (not pre-place/pre-optimization) and check for ECO/P&R insertions (buffer, gate sizing).
first_checks.why_first: stale netlist explains wholesale wrong sizes/extra devices and is cheap to verify

data.node_era_note: At 7nm-and-below, 'size' is quantized fin count (no continuous W) so size/extra mismatches are mostly fin-count/fin-cut Pcell quantization and standard-cell dummy/filler, whereas at 28nm planar, size mismatches are continuous drawn-W/effective-W rounding and gate-length bias.
data.symptom: (8) LVS mismatch: wrong device sizes or extra devices

data.alternatives_or_rejected: Conventional single-thread-optimized, deeply speculative, wide-issue out-of-order superscalar designs — the paper argues these spend area and power chasing instruction-level parallelism that commercial workloads do not offer.
data.decision: Optimize the whole processor for total throughput on commercial server workloads (database, web, Java/application-server class) rather than for the latency of one thread: many simple cores, many threads, low power per unit of work.
data.outcome: The paper reports a chip that delivers high throughput on commercial benchmarks (SPECjbb/SPECweb-class and TPC-C-like results) at a small fraction of the power of comparable conventional processors, while explicitly conceding poor single-thread performance.
data.rationale: As I recall the thrust of the argument: the target workloads have abundant thread-level parallelism but little instruction-level parallelism, and they stall on memory and long-latency events, so a conventional ILP machine leaves most of its machinery idle while burning power.
data.title: Design for throughput on commercial server workloads instead of single-thread performance
data.weakest_point: Whether the paper names any specific competing processor/microarchitecture it argues against, or only contrasts against the general class of ILP-optimized designs; my 'alternatives' phrasing may be broader than what the text actually says.
data.where_in_paper: Introduction / design philosophy or 'Why throughput computing' (opening section)

data.decision: Replicate a simple core eight times and give each core four hardware threads (32 threads/chip), with per-thread register state, all threads of a core sharing the core's execution units, L1 I-cache and L1 D-cache.
data.outcome: The paper reports that with four threads per core the core pipeline stays usefully busy under commercial workloads; I cannot recall a specific utilization or IPC figure stated in the paper.
data.rationale: My recollection of the stated reasoning: fine-grained multithreading hides both long memory latencies and pipeline/branch stalls by switching to another ready thread each cycle, so throughput is maintained without any of the speculation hardware a single-threaded core would need; four threads per core was the balance point between latency-hiding and the area/power cost of more thread state.
data.title: Four threads per core, eight cores, 32 threads; each thread gets its own register file
data.weakest_point: Whether the paper explicitly states a considered-and-rejected alternative (e.g. 'we evaluated eight threads per core and found diminishing returns') — I believe there is some discussion of the thread-count trade-off, but I cannot confirm the paper makes an explicit rejected-alternative argument, so I left that field as not-stated-in-paper.
data.where_in_paper: Multithreading / core architecture section (also the overview table near the front)

data.decision: Make each core single-issue and in-order with a short six-stage pipeline (fetch, thread-select, decode, execute, memory, writeback), with the integer/FP/memory functional units shared by the core's four threads, and a single floating-point unit per core because FP is rare in the target workloads.
data.outcome: The paper reports a core small enough to fit eight on the die within the power budget; it also notes the resulting weakness on floating-point / single-threaded SPECfp-class code.
data.rationale: Recollection of the thrust: area and power saved by omitting out-of-order issue, renaming and heavy speculation buys more cores and threads, which is where the throughput actually comes from; sharing the FP unit across threads costs little because commercial server code is mostly integer.
data.title: Simple single-issue, in-order, short-pipeline core with functional units shared across threads
data.weakest_point: Two sub-claims I am unsure the paper makes: (a) that there is no branch-prediction hardware at all and the short pipeline plus thread switching covers the branch delay — I believe Niagara omitted branch prediction, but I am not certain this paper says so in those words; (b) whether the shared FP unit is described as one per core or as one shared across larger groups of cores (I am ~75% sure it is one per core).
data.where_in_paper: SPARC core / pipeline description (with the six-stage pipeline figure)

data.decision: Give each core a small L1 instruction and data cache (write-through, no write-allocate, as I recall) and back all cores with a single shared, multi-banked L2 reached over a crossbar interconnect, so all memory traffic funnels through one on-chip coherence point.
data.outcome: The paper reports a shared L2 with high on-chip bandwidth (I cannot recall the GB/s figure as stated) and that the memory system, not the cores, sets the throughput ceiling on the commercial benchmarks.
data.rationale: Recollection of the thrust: keeping L1 small and write-through simplifies coherence and reduces the cost of the eight cache copies, while banking L2 and connecting it with a crossbar supplies the aggregate bandwidth that 32 threads demand; memory-level parallelism comes from threads rather than from prefetching or a large aggressive L1.
data.title: Shared, banked L2 reached through a crossbar, with small write-through L1 caches
data.weakest_point: The cache specifics: L1 sizes (I recall 16-Kbyte instruction / 8-Kbyte data per core), the number of L2 banks (I recall four), total L2 size (3 Mbyte), and especially the write-through/no-write-allocate claim — these are T1 facts I know generally and I am not certain which of them this 9-page paper actually states.
data.where_in_paper: Memory subsystem / cache and interconnect section

data.decision: Target a moderate clock frequency (Niagara shipped at about 1.2 GHz, in a 90-nm process) and hold the chip to a tight power envelope using extensive clock gating and power-aware design, accepting low single-thread speed in exchange for throughput per watt.
data.outcome: The paper reports a chip dissipating on the order of tens of watts (I recall a figure around 60-70 W but cannot trust my memory of the number as printed here) and uses it to claim a large throughput-per-watt advantage over conventional processors.
data.rationale: Recollection of the thrust: for these workloads the binding constraint is power, not die area or transistor count, so frequency and per-core complexity were deliberately capped and the saved power budget was spent on more cores and threads.
data.title: Moderate clock frequency and aggressive clock gating to hold the chip to a hard power budget
data.weakest_point: The wattage figure and the claimed power ratio versus competing chips — both are numbers I associate with T1 generally and I am not confident they appear as stated in this 2005 IEEE Micro paper, which was written close to (or before) silicon characterization.
data.where_in_paper: Power / implementation section (later in the paper, before or alongside the performance results)

data.alternatives_or_rejected: Conventional L1 I-cache holding x86 instruction bytes — not-stated-in-paper whether explicitly argued against
data.decision: Store decoded IA-32 micro-ops in a 12K-µop trace cache rather than a conventional L1 instruction cache; the IA-32 decoder is used only on trace-cache miss.
data.outcome: Trace cache achieves hit rate comparable to an 8–16 KB I-cache while bypassing decode; on miss, instructions are fetched from L2 and decoded.
data.rationale: Eliminates decode latency from the main execution loop and stores µops in program-flow (trace) order, increasing delivered instruction bandwidth to the execution core and aiding recovery from mispredicted branches.
data.title: Trace cache replaces conventional L1 instruction cache
data.weakest_point: Exact wording of the hit-rate comparison and whether the paper explicitly frames a conventional I-cache as a rejected alternative

data.alternatives_or_rejected: Shallower pipeline with more work per stage — not-stated-in-paper whether explicitly weighed
data.decision: Deepen pipeline to ~20 stages (vs. ~10 in P6) by simplifying each stage's work, trading higher branch-mispredict penalty for substantially higher achievable clock frequency.
data.outcome: Pentium 4 introduced at 1.5 GHz (November 2000); deep pipeline combined with enhanced branch prediction to mitigate mispredict penalty.
data.rationale: Simplified stage logic enables much higher clock rates; at 0.18 µm this allowed Pentium 4 to reach 1.5 GHz at introduction versus ~1 GHz limits for P6-based designs at the same process.
data.title: Very deep (20-stage) pipeline to maximize clock frequency
data.weakest_point: Whether the paper explicitly states the pipeline depth as a weighed decision against a shallower alternative, or simply describes it as a feature
data.where_in_paper: Overview of the NetBurst Microarchitecture / Hyper-Pipelined Technology

data.alternatives_or_rejected: Single-speed ALUs running at core clock — not-stated-in-paper whether explicitly considered
data.decision: Implement two ALUs and two AGUs that operate at twice the core clock frequency, executing one µop per half-cycle (rising and falling edge).
data.outcome: Four double-speed execution ports enable up to 6 µops per cycle to be dispatched; this offsets the IPC penalty of the deep pipeline for integer-heavy code.
data.rationale: To compensate for the longer pipeline's per-instruction latency and deliver high integer throughput; at 1.5 GHz core clock the ALUs effectively operate at 3 GHz, providing up to 6 µops/cycle peak issue bandwidth.
data.title: Double-pumped (2× clocked) ALUs — Rapid Execution Engine
data.weakest_point: Exact distribution of double-speed vs slow ALU and whether the paper frames this explicitly as a trade-off decision

data.alternatives_or_rejected: Traditional single-data-rate front-side bus synchronized to memory clock — not-stated-in-paper
data.decision: Use a 100 MHz external bus clock quad-pumped to deliver 400 MHz effective data rate, paired with dual-channel PC800 RDRAM for 3.2 GB/s peak bandwidth.
data.outcome: 400 MHz system bus delivers ~3× the bandwidth of the 133 MHz Pentium III FSB (1.06 GB/s → 3.2 GB/s).
data.rationale: Existing FSB speeds could not satisfy the bandwidth demands of the high-frequency core; quad-pumping decouples effective bus frequency from the physical pin clock.
data.title: 400 MHz system bus via quad-pumping
data.weakest_point: Whether the paper explicitly presents this as a design decision with rejected alternatives, or as a feature description

data.decision: Distribute a single global clock across the chip so that the two processor cores and the on-chip L2 operate synchronously at the same frequency, with clock skew budgeted and controlled in the distribution network, rather than bridging separately clocked islands with synchronizers or locally generated clocks.
data.outcome: The paper reports hardware that ran at/near its target frequency with measured skew within budget; I cannot recall specific ps or GHz figures stated here.
data.rationale: My recollection of the thrust of the argument: the core-to-L2 bandwidth is so high that synchronizer latency and clock-crossing uncertainty could not be afforded, and a single domain makes the entire chip timeable against one cycle; skew is then an engineering budget managed by balancing/tuning the distribution network.
data.title: One global clock domain for the cores and on-chip L2, with skew treated as a budgeted resource
data.weakest_point: The network topology detail (balanced tree vs. grid, tuned segments, 'local clock buffers') is general IBM/POWER4 practice, not something I can tie to this paper's text; and if the paper instead emphasizes multiple clock domains (e.g. L2 or the fabric interface at a divided frequency), my 'single domain' direction is reversed. I am only ~70% confident cores and L2 ran at the same frequency.
data.where_in_paper: Clock distribution section (a 'Clock distribution' / 'Clocking' topic area, later in the paper)

data.decision: Close timing using static timing analysis at the full-chip level, with each macro/unit carrying timing budgets or boundary timing contracts (arrival/required-time assertions) that could be renegotiated between units as the design converged, rather than signing off on the basis of simulated critical paths.
data.outcome: The paper reports the flow converged to tape-out and that first hardware met its frequency target; no quantitative closure results recalled.
data.rationale: As far as I can recall the thrust: simulation of a design this large cannot cover the path space, whereas STA gives complete coverage and explicit budgets let units be designed and closed somewhat independently and then integrated.
data.title: Full-chip static-timing sign-off with unit-level timing budgets / interface contracts
data.weakest_point: Whether tool names (e.g. IBM's EinsTimer) or the phrase 'timing assertions' actually appear here, and whether the paper frames this as a weighed decision at all — it may simply describe the flow. Very likely I am reconstructing a rationale the paper states differently.
data.where_in_paper: Timing methodology (design methodology / chip integration and timing-closure discussion)

data.decision: Design the on-chip power grid and its module/package connection against explicit IR-drop and current-density limits, i.e. treat power delivery and power density as design constraints during physical design rather than as a post-layout verification check.
data.outcome: The paper reports a very high chip power/dissipation figure (I believe in the ~100–120 W class) with measured drop within budget; I cannot recall the numbers as stated in this paper.
data.rationale: Recollection of thrust only: at this power level supply noise directly consumes timing margin and electromigration/current density bound the grid, so the grid had to be designed to a drop budget up front.
data.title: Power distribution, IR drop and power density treated as first-class physical-design constraints
data.weakest_point: Whether power/IR-drop has its own section in THIS paper or is mostly in the packaging/module companion material; the ~115 W number is general POWER4 knowledge and may not be stated here at all.
data.where_in_paper: Power distribution / power and thermal topic area (possibly overlapping packaging-module discussion)

data.decision: Implement the chip in IBM's 0.18 μm-class bulk CMOS with copper wiring and multiple metal levels (I do not recall the count), and size the wiring resource accordingly for a >1 GHz two-processor chip. I do not recall this being presented as a weighed choice with named rejected options.
data.outcome: The paper reports a very large transistor count (POWER4 is commonly cited at ~174 M transistors) on a single die; I cannot reliably recall the die size as given here.
data.rationale: Recollection of thrust: copper's lower resistance (and improved current-carrying capability) was what made the global wiring and power delivery feasible at this frequency and density — but I may be supplying this reasoning myself rather than recalling the paper's.
data.title: 0.18 μm bulk CMOS with copper interconnect as the technology base for the design
data.weakest_point: Everything quantitative: process name/generation, number of metal levels, whether low-k dielectric was used (I believe it was not at POWER4), and the die area (~267 mm²?) are all uncertain and drawn from general POWER4 knowledge rather than the paper text.
data.where_in_paper: Technology / process description (early section of the paper)

data.decision: Integrate two processor cores with a shared multi-banked on-chip L2 (with multiple L2 controllers) and an off-chip L3/fabric interface; the physical-design paper would only inherit this as a floorplanning input.
data.outcome: Not reported as an outcome in this paper.
data.rationale: This is microarchitecture rationale (throughput per chip, shared-L2 bandwidth), i.e. the companion paper's territory — I flag it rather than presenting it as content of this paper.
data.title: Two out-of-order cores plus shared on-chip L2, off-chip L3 and fabric bus
data.weakest_point: I cannot rule out that this paper's floorplan/integration section restates the core/L2 floorplan, in which case a floorplan-level version of it IS legitimately here — but the organizational description itself is the companion paper's.
data.where_in_paper: This belongs to the companion 'POWER4 system microarchitecture' paper (same issue, pp. 5–25), not to this circuit/physical-design paper — included only to mark the boundary
